primaryText: A dog appeared. It barked.
discourseSegments: A dog appeared.
It barked.
translation: A dog appeared. It barked.
comment: Syntactic scope anaphora: the indefinite's local variable is closed by the discourse-level summation over the world.

primaryText: Every farmer who owns a donkey pets it.
translation: Every farmer who owns a donkey pets it.
comment: Resumptive scope anaphora: the restriction label repeated in the nuclear scope closes the donkey variable for both indefinite and pronoun.

primaryText: Most dogs bark.
translation: Most dogs bark.
comment: A generalized quantifier as a relation between the summation of the restriction and of the restriction-plus-scope.

primaryText: Most farmers who own a donkey pet it.
translation: Most farmers who own a donkey pet it.

primaryText: Chris loves her.
translation: Chris loves her.
comment: The LF tree and the PIP tree of its meaning have the same shape.

primaryText: A red dog barked.
translation: A red dog barked.
comment: The tree whose interpretation introduces restricted variables and the operation FX.

primaryText: Every girl wrote a paper.
translation: Every girl wrote a paper.
comment: Quantifier raising inserts two summation operators labeled with the restriction set and the reference set.

primaryText: Most girls wrote a paper. All of them did something for a grade.
discourseSegments: Most girls wrote a paper.
All of them did something for a grade.
translation: Most girls wrote a paper. All of them did something for a grade.

primaryText: Most girls wrote a paper. But a few of them left it at home.
discourseSegments: Most girls wrote a paper.
But a few of them left it at home.
translation: Most girls wrote a paper. But a few of them left it at home.

readings.name: them = the girls that wrote a paper (the reference set)

primaryText: Most girls wrote a paper. In fact, they were mostly girls.
discourseSegments: Most girls wrote a paper.
In fact, they were mostly girls.
translation: Most girls wrote a paper. In fact, they were mostly girls.

readings.name: they = the individuals that wrote a paper (the scope set)

comment: No DP denotes the simple scope set, so it is not an antecedent.

primaryText: Every girl wrote a paper. They are on Ms. Marple's desk.
discourseSegments: Every girl wrote a paper.
They are on Ms. Marple's desk.
translation: Every girl wrote a paper. They are on Ms. Marple's desk.

readings.name: they = the papers the girls wrote

comment: The summation pronoun sums the paper variable of the reference-set label, presupposing plurality.

primaryText: Most dogs bark. They are loud.
discourseSegments: Most dogs bark.
They are loud.
translation: Most dogs bark. They are loud.

primaryText: Three students each wrote exactly two papers. They each sent them to L&P.
discourseSegments: Three students each wrote exactly two papers.
They each sent them to L&P.
translation: Three students each wrote exactly two papers. They each sent them to L&P.

readings.name: distributive: each student sent in their own two papers
collective over the papers: each student sent all six papers

comment: The collective reading, unavailable in Dynamic Plural Logic, is the summation pronoun over the papers written.

primaryText: Every parent who gives three balloons to two boys expects them to end up fighting (each other) for them.
translation: Every parent who gives three balloons to two boys expects them to end up fighting (each other) for them.

readings.name: collective: all the boys, all the balloons

comment: The collective reading is available but dispreferred without pragmatic support for the boys gathering.

primaryText: Every parent who had two children at Tappan Middle School was pleased when they (all) formed a rock band, the Tappin' Twofers, just for kids with siblings at the school.
translation: Every parent who had two children at Tappan Middle School was pleased when they (all) formed a rock band, the Tappin' Twofers, just for kids with siblings at the school.

primaryText: Everyone who ordered two or more drinks decided it was easier to just split the bill for them (all) evenly.
translation: Everyone who ordered two or more drinks decided it was easier to just split the bill for them (all) evenly.

primaryText: Some girls were having lunch in the cafeteria. They waved to some boys having lunch there, too.
discourseSegments: Some girls were having lunch in the cafeteria.
They waved to some boys having lunch there, too.
translation: Some girls were having lunch in the cafeteria. They waved to some boys having lunch there, too.

alternatives.form: Some girls were having lunch in the cafeteria. They waved to some other girls having lunch there, too.

comment: A simple pronoun to a weak indefinite is not exhaustive: other lunching girls may be mentioned.

primaryText: Most girls were having lunch in the cafeteria. They waved to some boys having lunch there, too.
discourseSegments: Most girls were having lunch in the cafeteria.
They waved to some boys having lunch there, too.
translation: Most girls were having lunch in the cafeteria. They waved to some boys having lunch there, too.

alternatives.form: Most girls were having lunch in the cafeteria. They waved to some other girls having lunch there, too.

comment: A summation pronoun is exhaustive: it denotes all the girls lunching, so 'other girls' lunching is infelicitous.

primaryText: The woman who saved her paycheck was wiser than the woman who spent it.
translation: The woman who saved her paycheck was wiser than the woman who spent it.

primaryText: Almost every girl brought the diorama she made to class. Very few of them forgot it at home.
discourseSegments: Almost every girl brought the diorama she made to class.
Very few of them forgot it at home.
translation: Almost every girl brought the diorama she made to class. Very few of them forgot it at home.

readings.name: it = the diorama made by each of the few

comment: The antecedent label contains the free variable of the girl, rebound by 'few'; the pronoun refers to dioramas not mentioned before.

primaryText: Everyone who owns an umbrella brought it to school today.
translation: Everyone who owns an umbrella brought it to school today.
context: Some people own more than one umbrella; each brought only one, or a few brought more than one.

readings.name: weak: one umbrella per owner suffices

primaryText: Everyone who owns an umbrella brought it to school today. They are in that rack.
discourseSegments: Everyone who owns an umbrella brought it to school today.
They are in that rack.
translation: Everyone who owns an umbrella brought it to school today. They are in that rack.
context: At least one person brought more than one umbrella.

readings.name: they = all the umbrellas actually brought, not one per owner

primaryText: Everyone who brought something valuable locked it up.
translation: Everyone who brought something valuable locked it up.
context: A few people brought more than one valuable item.

readings.name: strong: each locked up all their valuables

comment: The strong reading with the indefinite as a generalized quantifier and 'it' a summation pronoun over the valuables brought.

primaryText: Almost every student brought an umbrella today. Most (of them) used it, too.
discourseSegments: Almost every student brought an umbrella today.
Most (of them) used it, too.
translation: Almost every student brought an umbrella today. Most (of them) used it, too.
comment: The indefinite under the first quantifier antecedes a pronoun in the nuclear scope of the subordinate quantifier.

primaryText: Almost every student brought an umbrella today. Every one (of them) who used it stayed dry.
discourseSegments: Almost every student brought an umbrella today.
Every one (of them) who used it stayed dry.
translation: Almost every student brought an umbrella today. Every one (of them) who used it stayed dry.
comment: The novel observation: the pronoun may also appear in the subordinate quantifier's restriction.

primaryText: If she has a pet, it must be a donkey.
translation: If she has a pet, it must be a donkey.
comment: A conditional donkey sentence: the modal's nuclear scope is subordinate to its if-clause restriction.

primaryText: It might rain.
translation: It might rain.

primaryText: A wolf might enter. It would eat Tasty Tim first.
discourseSegments: A wolf might enter.
It would eat Tasty Tim first.
translation: A wolf might enter. It would eat Tasty Tim first.
comment: The second modal's restriction is anaphoric to the first's nuclear-scope label.

primaryText: He doesn't have a pen.
translation: He doesn't have a pen.
comment: Negation existentially closes the indefinite: summation over worlds.

primaryText: He doesn't own a car. It would be too expensive.
discourseSegments: He doesn't own a car.
It would be too expensive.
translation: He doesn't own a car. It would be too expensive.
comment: Negation antecedes modal subordination.

primaryText: It's not like he doesn't own a car. It is just in the shop.
discourseSegments: It's not like he doesn't own a car.
It is just in the shop.
translation: It's not like he doesn't own a car. It is just in the shop.
comment: Anaphora out of double negation: the label embedded under two negations is accessible to a summation pronoun.

primaryText: He doesn't own a car. It is in the shop.
discourseSegments: He doesn't own a car.
It is in the shop.
translation: He doesn't own a car. It is in the shop.
comment: The set of his cars is empty, so the pronoun's singular presupposition fails.

primaryText: Mary thinks I don't have a child, but I am a parent. He lives in England.
discourseSegments: Mary thinks I don't have a child, but I am a parent.
He lives in England.
translation: Mary thinks I don't have a child, but I am a parent. He lives in England.
context: Suggested by Matthew Mandelkern as a possible overgeneration.
comment: Odd through the difficulty of accommodating the gender and number presuppositions of 'he', not through inaccessibility of the label.

primaryText: Mary thinks I don't have a son, but she's wrong. She just hasn't met him yet.
discourseSegments: Mary thinks I don't have a son, but she's wrong.
She just hasn't met him yet.
translation: Mary thinks I don't have a son, but she's wrong. She just hasn't met him yet.

primaryText: Mary thinks I don't have any children, but I am actually a father several times over. She just hasn't ever met any of them!
discourseSegments: Mary thinks I don't have any children, but I am actually a father several times over.
She just hasn't ever met any of them!
translation: Mary thinks I don't have any children, but I am actually a father several times over. She just hasn't ever met any of them!

primaryText: Either there is no bathroom here or it's in a funny place.
translation: Either there is no bathroom here or it's in a funny place.
comment: Attributed to Barbara Partee; felicity reduces to: if there is a bathroom here, it is unique.

primaryText: Every monarchy cherishes its monarch.
translation: Every monarchy cherishes its monarch.
comment: No presupposition as a whole: the nuclear scope includes the restriction, which satisfies the pronoun's presupposition pointwise.

primaryText: Some people in my apartment building who own a bicycle own a car, too.
translation: Some people in my apartment building who own a bicycle own a car, too.

primaryText: Most of my friends who used to smoke have quit smoking by now.
translation: Most of my friends who used to smoke have quit smoking by now.

primaryText: John believes that Mary is the only one here, but he wishes that Susan were here too.
translation: John believes that Mary is the only one here, but he wishes that Susan were here too.
comment: The presupposition of 'too' under 'wishes' is satisfied by the label of the belief report, as in modal subordination.

primaryText: In the 1700s, every European country was a monarchy. Most of them cherished their monarchs.
discourseSegments: In the 1700s, every European country was a monarchy.
Most of them cherished their monarchs.
translation: In the 1700s, every European country was a monarchy. Most of them cherished their monarchs.
comment: Presupposition satisfaction across quantificational subordination: the first sentence's reference-set label is the second quantifier's restriction.

primaryText: Everyone in my apartment building owns a bicycle. Some of them own a car, too.
discourseSegments: Everyone in my apartment building owns a bicycle.
Some of them own a car, too.
translation: Everyone in my apartment building owns a bicycle. Some of them own a car, too.

primaryText: Every friend of mine used to smoke. But most of them have quit smoking by now.
discourseSegments: Every friend of mine used to smoke.
But most of them have quit smoking by now.
translation: Every friend of mine used to smoke. But most of them have quit smoking by now.
